**(B)** Intussusception

When a young cell elongates, its primary wall grows in surface area by intussusception: new wall material such as cellulose microfibrils is inserted into the existing wall, between the particles already there. Apposition is the laying of new layers one over another, which thickens the wall (as when the secondary wall is laid after growth stops), so it does not lengthen the cell. Super position is not a mode of wall growth.

[Note: the chapter does not state this; standard biology gives that surface growth of the wall is by intussusception and thickening is by apposition.]

**(D)** Proteins, Phospholipid and some carbohydrates

The chapter describes the cell membrane as a bilayer of lipids, mostly phospholipids, with proteins, and adds that it also contains carbohydrates (seen as glycoproteins and glycolipids in the fluid mosaic model). Options naming only two of these components are incomplete, and cellulose belongs to the plant cell wall, not to the membrane.

**(B)** Lipid

According to the fluid mosaic model, proteins float like icebergs in a sea of lipids. The chapter states that the quasifluid nature of the lipid enables lateral movement of proteins, and this movement is measured as fluidity. Carbohydrates, glycoproteins and polysaccharides sit on the membrane surface and do not make it fluid.

**(D)** All of the above

A plant cell has a cellulose cell wall, an algal cell has a wall of cellulose, galactans, mannans and minerals, and a prokaryotic cell has a cell wall of peptidoglycan as the middle layer of its cell envelope. Since all three named cells have a wall, the complete answer covers all of them.

**(A)** Selectively permeable

The chapter states that the main function of the plasma membrane is transport of molecules across it, and that this membrane is selectively permeable: it lets some substances pass freely, moves others by carriers or active transport, and keeps others out. It is not freely permeable or impermeable. A semipermeable membrane lets only the solvent through, which is how the chapter describes the tonoplast, not the plasma membrane.

**(D)** each one of the above

The chapter says the mitochondrial matrix contains a few coils of circular DNA. Like bacterial DNA, which mitochondria resemble under the endosymbiont theory, it is a double stranded molecule not associated with histone proteins, that is, naked. So all three descriptions apply.

[Note: the chapter does not state this; standard biology gives that mitochondrial DNA is naked, circular and double stranded.]

**(C)** Mitochondria, Chloroplast

Both mitochondria and chloroplasts are double membrane organelles that carry their own DNA and 70S ribosomes and can duplicate within the cell, which is the basis of the endosymbiont theory. Peroxisomes, the plasma membrane, ribosomes and the Golgi body contain no DNA, so every other pair includes at least one organelle without it.
